Use the finite graph phase data of [[def-qft-qed-finite-graph-gauge-data]] and the planned QED $U(1)$, Clifford, and natural-unit conventions of [[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]]. Let $K_0(\zeta)\in GL_d(\mathbb C)$ be an invertible base matrix and let $V(\zeta)\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ be its finite link-hopping matrix. The admissible covariant families satisfy
$$
K_0(\zeta^\alpha)=D_\alpha K_0(\zeta)D_\alpha^{-1},\qquad
V(\zeta^\alpha)=D_\alpha V(\zeta)D_\alpha^{-1}.
$$
The scalar base $K_0=mI_d$, $m\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$, is an explicit admissible case. Define
$$
K(z;\zeta):=K_0(\zeta)+zV(\zeta),\qquad
S(z;\zeta):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-zK_0(\zeta)^{-1}V(\zeta))^nK_0(\zeta)^{-1}.
$$
The coefficient of each power $z^n$ in $S$ is one finite matrix. The item defines this formal candidate; the following lemma proves its two-sided inverse and covariance properties. Define $\det A$ for a finite matrix $A$ over $\mathbb C\llbracket z\rrbracket$ by the Leibniz formula $\det A=\sum_{\sigma\in S_d}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{j=1}^d A_{j,\sigma(j)}$.

For a real vertex phase $\theta=(\theta_x)_{x\in X}\in\mathbb R^X$, define
$$
\zeta_e^\theta:=e^{i(\theta_{s(e)}-\theta_{t(e)})}\zeta_e,\qquad
D_\theta:=\operatorname{diag}_{x\in X}(e^{i\theta_x}I_r)\in GL_d(\mathbb C).
$$
Define the link-hopping matrix $V(\zeta)\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ by its $x,y$ block indexed by $x,y\in X$
$$
V(\zeta)_{xy}:=\sum_{\substack{e\in E\\s(e)=x,\ t(e)=y}}T_e\zeta_e .
$$
An empty sum is the zero $r\times r$ matrix. Additional fixed diagonal blocks belong to a separate base matrix. These data are finite-dimensional algebraic data; the phases are external parameters, not rotor multiplication operators on $L^2(\mathbb T^E)$.

For a real smooth gauge parameter $\chi$ in webers, put $\alpha=\chi/S_0$ (dimensionless) and use
$$A'_a=A_a+\partial_a\chi,\qquad a'_a=a_a+\partial_a\alpha,\qquad \psi'=e^{ig\alpha}\psi.$$
The induced covariant derivative is $D'_a=\partial_a-ig a'_a$. These are formal mathematical conventions for the later conditional deductions. They do not adopt a measured value of $\mu_0$, identify $q$ with an electron charge, impose charge quantization, or assert that interacting continuum fields exist.

derivations.claim: Put $B:=K_0^{-1}V$. The coefficient of $z^n$ in $S$ is $(-B)^nK_0^{-1}$, a finite matrix, so the series defines an element of $M_d(\mathbb C[[z]])$ without an analytic convergence assumption.

Since $K=K_0(I+zB)$, multiplication gives $KS=K_0(I+zB)\sum_{n\ge0}(-zB)^nK_0^{-1}$. In the product $(I+zB)\sum_{n\ge0}(-zB)^n$, the constant coefficient is $I$ and the two contributions to every positive-degree coefficient cancel; hence $KS=I$.
Also $K_0^{-1}K=I+zB$, so $SK=\sum_{n\ge0}(-zB)^n(I+zB)=I$ by the same coefficientwise cancellation. Thus $S$ is the two-sided formal inverse.

Each link block transforms as $T_e\zeta_e^\theta=e^{i\theta_{s(e)}}(T_e\zeta_e)e^{-i\theta_{t(e)}}$; summing links in each block gives $V(\zeta^\theta)=D_\theta V(\zeta)D_\theta^{-1}$. With [A1], the assumed covariance of $K_0$ gives the same conjugation for each coefficient of $K$; the QED phase interpretation is exactly $\theta_x=g\alpha_x$ from [F3].
Substituting the conjugated $K_0,V$ into the defining series for $S$ conjugates each finite coefficient by $D_\theta$, proving $S(z;\zeta^\theta)=D_\theta S(z;\zeta)D_\theta^{-1}$.
Differentiate $K_sS_s=I$ coefficientwise at $s=0$. This gives $(\delta K)S+K(\delta S)=0$, hence $\delta S=-S(\delta K)S$ using $K^{-1}=S$.
From $D_s=e^{is\Theta}$, direct differentiation gives $\delta K=i[\Theta,K]$. Therefore $-S\,i[\Theta,K]\,S=-iS\Theta KS+iSK\Theta S=-iS\Theta+i\Theta S=i[\Theta,S]$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

Use the transverse space $\mathcal H_T=\operatorname{Ran}M_{P_T}$ of [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]], with $P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-\mathbf n\mathbf n^T$ for $\mathbf k\ne0$ and any assigned value at the null point $\mathbf k=0$. In the QFT length convention, assign $\mathbf k$ units m$^{-1}$ and define the nonnegative measurable multiplier
$$
\omega(\mathbf k):=|\mathbf k|.
$$
Its maximal multiplication operator on $\mathcal H_T$ is
$$
(M_\omega f)(\mathbf k):=\omega(\mathbf k)f(\mathbf k),\qquad
D(M_\omega):=\{f\in\mathcal H_T:\omega f\in L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3)\}.
$$
Because $\omega$ is a scalar multiplier, $\mathbf k\cdot f(\mathbf k)=0$ a.e. implies $\mathbf k\cdot(M_\omega f)(\mathbf k)=0$ a.e.; thus the displayed multiplication maps its stated domain into $\mathcal H_T$. The value $\omega(0)=0$ is immaterial to the $L^2$ operator. For $\hbar,c>0$, the corresponding one-particle energy convention is $E_1:=\hbar c M_\omega$, in joules.

Define $\epsilon(z)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}z^{\otimes n}/\sqrt{n!}$ for $z\in H$.
There are unitaries $W(h)$ determined on these total exponential vectors by
$$W(h)\epsilon(z)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|h\|^2}{4} +\frac{i}{\sqrt2}\langle h,z\rangle_2\right) \epsilon\!\left(z+\frac{i h}{\sqrt2}\right).$$
They obey
$$W(h)W(k)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{i}{2}\operatorname{Im}\langle h,k\rangle_2\right)W(h+k),\qquad \langle\Omega,W(h)\Omega\rangle_2=e^{-\|h\|^2/4},$$
and $h\mapsto W(h)$ is strongly continuous. For every $h$, the one-parameter
group $t\mapsto W(th)$ has norm derivative at zero exactly on
$D(\Phi(h))$, with derivative $i\Phi(h)$ (for $h=0$ this is the zero
generator). Thus the displayed bounded Weyl operators have precisely the
closed Segal fields as their generators; no point-field or measurement claim
is included.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space and let
$\boldsymbol\omega=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_d):X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a
finite-valued measurable map, where $d\ge1$. Put
$H=L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ with the second-variable-linear pairing of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and form the bosonic Fock space
$\mathcal F_s(H)$. For $n\ge1$, identify $H_s^{(n)}$ with the symmetric
subspace of $L^2(X^n,\overline{\mu^{\times n}};\mathbb C)$ by iterating
[[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]]. Set $X^0=\{\star\}$,
$s_0(\star)=0$, and for $n\ge1$ set
$$s_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{r=1}^n\boldsymbol\omega(x_r)\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For $1\le j\le d$, define $H_j$ by multiplication by the $j$th coordinate
$s_{n,j}$ on sector $n$, with exact domain
$$D(H_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n): \sum_{n\ge1}\int_{X^n}|s_{n,j}|^2|\Psi_n|^2\,d\overline{\mu^{\times n}}<\infty\right\}.$$
Each $H_j$ is self-adjoint, and $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\cap D(H_j)$ is a
graph core. The joint projection-valued measure
[[def-projection-valued-measure]] on $\mathbb R^d$ is
$$(E(B)\Psi)_n=\mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B)}\Psi_n\quad(n\ge1),\qquad (E(B)\Psi)_0=\mathbf1_B(0)\Psi_0.$$
For $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, let $H_\theta$ be multiplication on sector $n$
by $\theta\cdot s_n$, with its maximal square-integrability domain. Then
$$U_\theta(t)\Psi:=\bigl(e^{it\theta\cdot s_n}\Psi_n\bigr)_{n\ge0}$$
is a strongly continuous unitary group on all of Fock space, and its norm
derivative at zero exists exactly for $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$, where it is
$iH_\theta\Psi$. The zero-particle sector is the vacuum eigenvector at joint
value $0$.

derivations.claim: For $\mathbf n\in S^2$, $P_T(\mathbf n)=I-\mathbf n\mathbf n^\top$ is an orthogonal projection and [A2] gives $\mathbf n\cdot b(\mathbf n)=0$; hence $\mathbf k\cdot f_\epsilon(\mathbf k)=0$ a.e. Since $\epsilon<|\mathbf k|<\kappa$ on the support, both $f_\epsilon$ and $\omega f_\epsilon$ are square-integrable.

In spherical coordinates $d^3k=r^2dr\,d\Omega$, so $\|f_\epsilon\|^2=C_b\int_\epsilon^\kappa r^{-1}dr=C_b\log(\kappa/\epsilon)$, $\langle f_\epsilon,\omega f_\epsilon\rangle=C_b(\kappa-\epsilon)$, and $\|\omega f_\epsilon\|^2=C_b(\kappa^2-\epsilon^2)/2$.

On the full vector space $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$, multiplication by $\omega$ commutes with the multiplier $P_T$. Its tensor-power projections therefore commute with the sector multiplier $\sum_j|\mathbf k_j|$; the transverse symmetric Fock space is a reducing subspace for the second-quantized multiplier of [F3]. If $r=\|f_\epsilon\|^2$, $q=\langle f_\epsilon,\omega f_\epsilon\rangle$, and $s=\|\omega f_\epsilon\|^2$, the sector formulas give
$
\|d\Gamma(\omega)C(f_\epsilon)\|^2
=e^{-r}\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{n s r^{n-1}+n(n-1)q^2r^{n-2}}{n!}
=s+q^2<\infty.
$
The same sector sum with one multiplier gives $\langle C(f_\epsilon),d\Gamma(\omega)C(f_\epsilon)\rangle=q$; [F2] gives $\|C(f_\epsilon)\|=1$. Multiplying by $\hbar c$ and substituting [step 1.2] proves the stated domain and energy claims.

Put $\epsilon_j=\kappa e^{-j}$ for $j\ge1$. The difference $f_{\epsilon_{j+1}}-f_{\epsilon_j}$ is supported on the shell $(\epsilon_{j+1},\epsilon_j)$, so its squared norm is $C_b\int_{\epsilon_{j+1}}^{\epsilon_j}r^{-1}dr=C_b$. From [F2],
$
|\langle C(f_{\epsilon_j}),C(f_{\epsilon_{j+1}})\rangle|
=e^{-\|f_{\epsilon_{j+1}}-f_{\epsilon_j}\|^2/2}=e^{-C_b/2}<1.
$
Thus $\|C(f_{\epsilon_j})-C(f_{\epsilon_{j+1}})\|^2\ge2(1-e^{-C_b/2})>0$, and this sequence is not Cauchy.

Let $\Psi$ have only sectors $0,\ldots,N$. Then
$
|\langle\Psi,C(f_\epsilon)\rangle|
\le e^{-\|f_\epsilon\|^2/2}\sum_{n=0}^{N}\frac{\|\Psi_n\|\|f_\epsilon\|^n}{\sqrt{n!}}\longrightarrow0
$
as $\epsilon\downarrow0$, because [step 1.2] gives $\|f_\epsilon\|\to\infty$ and the exponential dominates this fixed polynomial. Finite-sector vectors are dense: for any Fock vector $\Psi=(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}$, the truncations $\sum_{n=0}^N\Psi_n$ converge in norm because $\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty$. Since $\|C(f_\epsilon)\|=1$, approximation gives weak convergence to zero for every Fock vector. A norm limit would have to equal the weak limit zero, contradicting the unit norms.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

$$

$$
and let $[M_d]P\in R$ denote the coefficient of $M_d$ in $P\in\Lambda_d(R)$. Define the finite Grassmann integral by the $R$-linear functional
$$
\mathcal I_d(P):=(-1)^{d(d+1)/2}[M_d]P .
$$
For $K\in M_d(R)$, put $B_K:=\sum_{i,j=1}^d\bar\psi_iK_{ij}\psi_j$. Since every monomial of degree greater than $2d$ vanishes, its exponential is the finite sum
$$
\exp(-B_K):=\sum_{n=0}^{d}\frac{(-B_K)^n}{n!}.
$$
The sign factor in $\mathcal I_d$ is the chosen normalization. Its Gaussian determinant identity, including the value at $K=I_d$, is proved separately.

$$
K_0(\zeta^\alpha)=D_\alpha K_0(\zeta)D_\alpha^{-1},\qquad
V(\zeta^\alpha)=D_\alpha V(\zeta)D_\alpha^{-1}.
$$
The scalar base $K_0=mI_d$, $m\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$, is an explicit admissible case. Define
$$

S(z;\zeta):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-zK_0(\zeta)^{-1}V(\zeta))^nK_0(\zeta)^{-1}.
$$

$$\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3),\qquad
\langle u,v\rangle_2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\overline{u(\mathbf k)}\cdot v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,$$
with the second-variable-linear convention of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]; the dot product and norm on each $\mathbb R^3$ fiber are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and Hilbert completeness follows from [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For $\mathbf k\ne0$, write $n(\mathbf k)=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and
$$P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-n(\mathbf k)n(\mathbf k)^T.$$
Assign any value at $\mathbf k=0$, which is a Lebesgue-null set. Let $M_{P_T}$ be multiplication by this measurable matrix field and define the positive transverse photon space
$$\mathcal H_T=\operatorname{Ran}M_{P_T}
=\{u\in\mathcal H:\mathbf k\cdot u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ for almost every }\mathbf k\ne0\}.$$
The inner product on $\mathcal H_T$ is the restriction of that on $\mathcal H$. Each nonzero momentum fiber is the two-dimensional plane perpendicular to $\mathbf k$; no global continuous polarization frame is part of the definition.
